demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Here is the clinical vignette based on the details provided.

Three months ago, he was working the afternoon shift on a commercial rooftop unit near downtown. The job was straightforward: replace a failed compressor on a four-ton package unit. He had done it dozens of times before. He remembers the heat that day-the asphalt roof baking under a cloudless sky, the growl of the condenser fan, the sharp smell of refrigerant cutting through the August air. He was on the last step, guiding the new compressor into the access panel, when a nearby service valve suddenly blew. The old technician-a man named Frank, who had been showing him the building's system map-was standing too close. A high-pressure jet of R-22 hit Frank's right eye before he could turn away. Frank screamed, dropped to his knees, and covered his face. The sound of that scream still wakes him at 3:17 every morning.

Now, every time he climbs onto a roof, his hands shake. He checks service valves three times, then a fourth, and still he cannot trust them. Last week he was changing a filter for a regular client-a small job he could do in his sleep-and when he cracked the service port to check pressure, the hiss of escaping gas sent him reeling backward off his ladder. He caught himself, but he stood there on the ground for fifteen minutes, heart thudding, unable to go back up. His supervisor told him to take a day off; the company doesn't want anyone getting hurt. He took the day, but the next morning he felt a knot in his stomach just from looking at his work van.

He no longer drives past the medical clinic where Frank was airlifted that afternoon. He takes three extra streets to avoid it, even if it makes him late. He also avoids the tool aisle at the supply house where he used to buy copper tubing and brazing rods-there, in the back, is the same brand of service valve that failed. He finds reasons to stay on the ground: volunteering to check ductwork in crawlspaces, offering to clean evap coils on ground-level units. Anything to keep off a roof. His coworker Jorge has started covering the rooftop calls for him, but Jorge doesn't know why. No one does. He told the foreman it was a "balance thing," and the foreman shrugged. That seems to be enough.

At home, he lives with his mother and younger sister in a small two-bedroom apartment. He used to spend Saturday afternoons tuning up the window units for neighbors-a favor, a way to stay sharp. Now he ignores their texts. His mother asks why he is so quiet. He says he is tired. He does not tell her about the images that flicker into his mind unbidden: the spray of oil, the way Frank's hands came up too late, the blood on the granite roof gravel. He has stopped sleeping in his bed. The bed is too soft; he never feels safe. Instead he sleeps on the living-room couch, fully dressed, with his work boots near the door. That way he can get up and leave quickly if he needs to. He does not know from what.

The memories arrive without warning. In the middle of a normal day-waiting for the subway, eating a burrito, checking his phone-he will suddenly smell refrigerant oil. He knows it is not real, but he gags anyway. He has lost weight. He no longer jokes with customers. He completes jobs in silence, leaving before the homeowner can ask a follow-up question. Yesterday he stood in front of the supply house for twenty minutes, unable to open the door, because inside he might see a man in blue coveralls and remember Frank's eye-the red, the way Frank had tried to stand and then fell again. He turned around and went home.

He has not called Frank to apologize. He cannot. The thought of hearing Frank's voice makes his throat close. He has written the number down three times and deleted it three times. He hopes Frank is okay, but he does not check. He is afraid of what he will find. At night, lying on the couch, he replays the moment again and again, looking for a way it could have been different. Maybe if he had used a different wrench. Maybe if he had told Frank to stand back. There is never a version where Frank does not scream.
